questions.q: Which of these is not one of the three things every recursive function needs?
questions.explain: Base case, smaller step and combine step are the whole recipe. A depth counter can be useful (as a parameter), but it is not required, and a global one is shared by every call, which causes bugs.
options: A base case you can answer directly
A step that turns the input into a smaller input of the same kind
A way to combine the smaller answers into this answer
A global variable that counts how deep the recursion is

questions.q: folderSize adds a folder's files, then calls itself for each sub-folder. It has no if. Why does it still stop?
questions.explain: Recursion over a tree stops where the tree stops. A leaf (no children) is the base case, handled by a loop over an empty list.
options: JavaScript stops any function after 100 recursive calls
For a folder without sub-folders the loop runs zero times, so that call returns without calling itself: the base case is in the data
It does not stop; it only works because the data is small
for...of loops cannot contain recursive calls

questions.q: When you write the combine step of a recursive function, what should you assume?
questions.explain: This "leap of faith" is the same reasoning as proof by induction. If the base case is correct and each call gets closer to it, the function is correct at any depth.
options: Nothing: you must trace every level by hand to be sure
That the function already returns the right answer for the smaller pieces; you only check that the base case is right and always reached
That the input is never deeper than two levels
That the function will be memoized

questions.q: countPeople declares let total = 1 and then adds the results of its recursive calls. While the deepest call runs, how many total variables exist?
questions.explain: Every call has its own execution context with its own local variables. The waiting calls keep their half-finished total until the call above them returns.
options: One, shared by every call
One per call that is still on the stack; each call has its own
Two: one for the first call and one for all the others
None: local variables are removed during recursion

questions.q: In a recursive walk of an org chart, which call returns first?
questions.explain: A call cannot finish until all the calls it made have finished. The first to finish is the first one that makes no further calls, and results then flow back up the stack.
options: The call for the CEO, at the top
The first call that reaches a person with no reports, deepest on its branch
The call for the last person in the input array
All calls return at the same moment

questions.q: To delete a folder, each folder must be emptied before it is removed. Which order does your recursive function need?
questions.explain: Post-order puts the work after the recursive calls, so all children are handled before their parent. Pre-order would try to remove a folder that still has contents.
options: Pre-order: handle the folder, then its sub-folders
Post-order: handle the sub-folders first, then the folder
Level order with a queue
Any order works

questions.q: function preOrder(node, out = []) { out.push(node.name); for (const c of node.children) preOrder(c, out); return out; }. What role does out play?
questions.explain: The top-level call creates the array (by the default), and every recursive call receives the same array as an argument. The alternative is for each call to return its own list and combine them.
options: It is a cache of earlier results
It is an accumulator: one array passed down to every call so they all add to the same result
It is a stack that replaces the call stack
It counts the depth

questions.q: In pathTo(person, target), the loop does const path = pathTo(report, target); if (path !== null) return [person.name, ...path];. What goes wrong if you write return [person.name, ...pathTo(report, target)] instead?
questions.explain: A search must try the next branch when one fails. Returning unconditionally ends the loop after the first report; spreading a null result into an array throws a TypeError.
options: Nothing; it is just shorter
It returns after searching only the first report, even when the target is under a later one, and spreading null throws
It searches every report twice
It never reaches the base case

questions.q: Why is if (n <= 0) usually a safer base case than if (n === 0)?
questions.explain: A base case must be reached from every valid input. Covering a range protects you from inputs that step past the single value you expected.
options: <= is faster than ===
If the step can jump over 0 (a negative start, steps of 2 from an odd number, a fraction), === 0 is never true and the recursion never stops
=== does not work with numbers
There is no difference

questions.q: A recursive size function calls itself for each sub-folder but forgets to add the returned value. What is the symptom?
questions.explain: The recursive calls run and return their answers, which are then thrown away. Silent wrong answers are the most dangerous bugs; tests with nested data catch them.
options: A RangeError
A SyntaxError
No error at all, just a total that only counts the top folder's own files
The function returns undefined

questions.q: A report count over the org chart suddenly throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, although the company has only 40 people. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Recursion over a tree assumes no item is its own ancestor. A cycle turns a 40-person walk into an endless one. Track visited people in a Set and report the cycle.
options: 40 people is too many for recursion
The data has a cycle: someone's reports lead back to one of their own managers, so the walk goes round forever
A person has no reports
Names contain spaces

questions.q: Cycle detection stores visited people in a Set. Why is it right that a Set compares objects by identity here?
questions.explain: Storing names would wrongly flag two different employees who share a name. Identity answers the real question: have I been at this exact node before?
options: Because two people can never have the same name
A cycle means meeting the very same object again; identity recognises exactly that, while two different people with equal data are not a cycle
Because sets cannot store objects by content
Identity is not right; the set should store names

questions.q: ways(n) returns ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2). For n = 40 it takes seconds. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: ways(38) is computed twice, ways(37) three times, and so on. Caching each result makes the count linear, as the lesson's 242,785 calls versus 49 calls showed.
options: The base case is wrong; change it to n <= 2
The two calls overlap and recompute the same values again and again, so the call count grows exponentially; memoize it
Recursion is always slow; rewrite it as a loop
The stack is too small; increase it
Numbers above 32 are slow in JavaScript

questions.q: Roughly how deep can a simple recursive function go in Node.js or Chrome before RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded?
questions.explain: The stack is small compared with the heap. Folder trees and menus are nowhere near the limit; chains of records and user-controlled nesting can be.
options: About 100 calls
On the order of ten thousand calls, depending on the engine and how much each call stores
About ten million calls
There is no limit

questions.q: A function ends with return total(entry.previous, sum + entry.amountKobo), a tail call. Does that protect it from stack overflow in Node.js?
questions.explain: You cannot rely on tail call elimination in the engines you deploy on: only JavaScriptCore, Safari's engine, implements proper tail calls. For data that can be arbitrarily deep, use a loop or an explicit stack.
options: Yes, JavaScript always reuses the frame for tail calls
No: the specification describes proper tail calls, but V8 (Node.js and Chrome) does not implement them, so every call still takes a frame
Yes, but only for arrow functions
Only in strict mode

questions.q: Why does rewriting a recursive walk with an array used as a stack remove the depth limit?
questions.explain: Recursion keeps "what is still to do" in stack frames. An explicit stack keeps the same information in a heap array, whose size is limited only by memory.
options: Arrays are faster than function calls
The to-do list lives in an ordinary array on the heap, which can hold millions of items, instead of in call-stack frames
pop clears the call stack
It does not remove the limit; it only hides the error

questions.q: In an explicit-stack walk, what changes if you take work from the front with shift() instead of the end with pop()?
questions.explain: A stack (last in, first out) goes deep first. A queue (first in, first out) finishes a whole level before the next, which answers "who reports directly to the CEO, then who reports to them".
options: Nothing
The walk visits nodes in reverse alphabetical order
It becomes a queue, so the tree is visited level by level (breadth-first) instead of branch by branch (depth-first)
It visits each node twice

questions.q: Comment rows arrive from the database in any order, each with an id and a parentId. Why does buildThread first put every row in a Map and only then attach children?
questions.explain: Two passes make the order of the rows irrelevant and need no recursion at all, so building the tree cannot overflow the stack however deep the thread is.
options: Because maps are required for recursion
So a reply can be attached even when its row comes before its parent's row: in the second pass every parent is already in the map
To sort the comments by date
To make a deep copy of every row

questions.q: Your API walks the JSON body of each request with an unlimited recursive function. What is the production risk?
questions.explain: Data from users can be as deep as they like. Any recursion over it needs a depth limit, or an explicit stack, so that bad input produces a clean validation error instead of a crash.
options: None: request bodies are always shallow
A client can send deeply nested JSON that overflows the stack, so each such request throws a RangeError in your code; cap the depth or iterate
Recursion leaks the request body to other users
JSON cannot be walked recursively

questions.q: balanceAfter(months) can be written recursively or with a for loop over the months. Which is usually the better choice, and why?
questions.explain: Recursion earns its place on data that contains smaller copies of itself. For a count of months, a loop is the natural tool.
options: Recursion, because it is always shorter
The loop: the data is a simple sequence, not nested, so a loop is at least as clear and has no depth limit
Recursion, because loops cannot compute interest
Both are equally risky

questions.q: In deepEqual(a, b) for JSON data, what is the base case?
questions.explain: Objects and arrays are the branches of a JSON tree; primitives are the leaves. Leaves are compared directly, and branches compare each key by calling deepEqual again. (Identity is a useful shortcut, but not the base case that ends the walk.)
options: Both values are arrays
At least one of the values is not an object (a primitive or null): compare directly and stop
Both objects have more than ten keys
The two objects are identical

questions.q: You need the number of replies under a comment in a table of 20 million comments. What is the better design?
questions.explain: Loading millions of rows to count a few is wasteful. SQL databases can walk trees themselves with WITH RECURSIVE, close to the data.
options: Load all rows into memory, build the tree and count recursively
Let the database walk the parent/child rows with a recursive SQL query, and return just the count
Call the API once per comment
Increase the stack size and recurse

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10. A negative start hits the n <= 0 base case immediately.
options: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A's call starts, then runs B's call to completion, then C's, and only then prints its own out. A child's whole call happens inside its parent's call.
options:
in A
in B
out B
in C
out C
out A

in A
out A
in B
out B
in C
out C

in A
in B
in C
out C
out B
out A

in B
out B
in C
out C
in A
out A

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The node's own name comes first, then each child's whole list in turn: pre-order. Level order would print Drinks before Rice.
options: Shop, Food, Rice, Drinks
Rice, Food, Drinks, Shop
Shop, Food, Drinks, Rice
Food, Rice, Drinks

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every node's children come before the node itself: post-order. Rice comes before Food, and both before Drinks, because Food's whole subtree is finished before Drinks starts.
options: Rice, Food, Drinks, Shop
Shop, Food, Rice, Drinks
Drinks, Rice, Food, Shop
Rice, Drinks, Food, Shop

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only non-array items count as 1; arrays are opened and their contents counted. The items are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The empty array adds 0.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The recursive calls run, but their return values are thrown away. Only the top folder's own 10 is returned. The fix is sum += total(sub).
options: undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: From 6 the steps reach 0. From 7 they go 5, 3, 1, -1 and skip 0 for ever, until the stack overflows. n <= 0 would stop both.
options:
done
RangeError

done
done
RangeError

done
TypeError

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The search under Tunde returns null, so the loop moves on to Bola. Each level puts its own name in front of the path from below. Nobody matches Zainab, so every level returns null.
options: [ 'Ngozi', 'Bola', 'Funmi' ] null
[ 'Funmi', 'Bola', 'Ngozi' ] null
[ 'Ngozi', 'Tunde', 'Bola', 'Funmi' ] null
[ 'Ngozi', 'Bola', 'Funmi' ] []

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A leaf has depth 1. Every other node is 1 more than its deepest child. The second child's branch goes three levels below the root, so the root's depth is 4.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ways(5) is 8, but getting there takes 15 calls, because smaller values are computed again and again. That repeated work is what memoization removes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With shift the list is a queue: A, then its children B and C, then D (level order). With pop it is a stack: after A, the last child C comes out first, then B, then D.
options: ABCD ACBD
ABDC ABDC
ABCD ABDC
ACBD ABCD

questions.q: Default parameters are evaluated on every call. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each top-level call gets a fresh [] from the default, and recursive calls receive that same array explicitly. The two results do not share an accumulator.

questions.q: Write the recursive folderSize(folder): the sum of the kb of its files plus the size of every sub-folder, at any depth.
questions.explain: Add this folder's files, then trust folderSize for each sub-folder and add its answer. A folder without sub-folders is the base case: the second loop does nothing.

questions.q: Write countComments(comments) that counts every comment in a list, including all replies at any depth.
questions.explain: Each comment counts 1 plus everything in its replies. An empty list is the base case and counts 0.

questions.q: Write maxDepth(category): a category with no children has depth 1; otherwise its depth is 1 more than its deepest child.
questions.explain: Starting deepest at 0 makes a leaf return 1 without a special case. Each level adds 1 to the deepest answer from below.

questions.q: Write a recursive flattenAll(list) that turns nested arrays of any depth into one flat array, keeping the order. Do not use the built-in flat.
questions.explain: A non-array item is a leaf and goes straight into the result. An array is a smaller problem of the same kind: flatten it and add its items. (list.flat(Infinity) does the same thing built in.)

questions.q: Write findById(node, id) for a category tree: return the node whose id matches, searching all levels, or null if there is none.
questions.explain: Return as soon as a branch finds the node, but only when it really found it: a null from one child means "try the next child".

questions.q: Write sumNested(list) without recursion: use an array as an explicit stack to add up every number in nested arrays of any depth. It must handle 50,000 levels of nesting.
questions.explain: Instead of calling itself for an inner array, the function pushes it onto a to-do stack and handles it later in the same loop. The stack is a heap array, so depth no longer matters; the recursive starter overflows on the deep input.

questions.q: Write breadcrumbs(category, trail) returning one string per category, in pre-order, such as Food > Grains > Rice. Build a new trail array for each call instead of changing a shared one.
questions.explain: Each call copies the trail and adds its own name, so siblings never see each other's names. Pushing into one shared trail would turn "Food > Oils" into "Food > Grains > Rice > Oils".
questions.expected: Food | Food > Grains | Food > Grains > Rice | Food > Oils
